description.narrative: CMI!’s vision is a gender-equal and just world, where all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people enjoy their rights fully and live to their full potential. Our role in bringing about this vision is to support movements to be resilient and leverage their power to create change from local to global, and from global to local, thereby engendering systemic and sustainable change at all levels.

In order for feminist civil society movements to be strong and autonomous39 (an ambitious achievement in itself), self-led WHRDs and WROs go through three intermediate steps - resulting in CMI!’s output (see section 4 and Annex 1, our Results Framework). WHRDs and WROs must be: RESOURCED with the knowledge, resources, and skills for impact, including for L&A. COORDINATED to be able to organise together to articulate priorities and take collective action, including amplifying voices through alliances between structurally excluded movements, linking with more mainstream movements where possible. RESILIENT by having resources, networks, strength and holistic security in place to sustain their work including in the face of backlash and closing civic space, build broader support bases, and expand their work.

Our five-year strategic objective is: political actors, societal actors and donors at local, national, regional and global levels take action to recognise, protect and fulfil the human rights of all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people as a result of strong and autonomous feminist movements holding them to account.

WO=MEN has engaged with the WTO Gender Unit during several meetings in which WO=MEN stressed the importance of structural engagement with women's rights organisations and the creation of space for meaningful participation. This result follows several years of engagement with the WTO Gender Unit, including a presentation by WO=MEN on 6 December 2022 during the first World Trade Congress on Gender about the inclusion of women's rights organisations in trade policy development. During the WTO Public Forum in 2023, WO=MEN participated on behalf of CMI! and organised a knowledge-sharing session with the head of the Gender Unit of the WTO about the importance of collaborating with women's rights organisations. This is particularly important as there is very little space for the engagement of civil society, particularly for women's rights organisations, in the decision-making processes of the WTO. International feminist movements are very critical of the WTO and are concerned that any WTO initiatives related to gender equality will be nothing more than pinkwashing. For this reason, it's even more important that civil society organisations, including women's rights organisations, can be watchdogs in WTO spaces, making this new commitment from WTO particularly relevant and important. By participating in and following up on the WTO Public Forum 2023, organising a session jointly with the CMI Feminist Economic Realities working group and other engagements internationally on economic alternatives and in WTO spaces, WO=MEN has strengthened its alliances with other actors - NGOs, academia - working in the area of sustainable economic developments and alternatives.

This reporting measure of this indicator is unique. New or strengthened alliances at different levels will be captured. In case one alliance is created in the first year, we shall only count for that year regardless of the number of times activities will be carried out to strengthen that alliance.

Although the actual ratification of ILO Convention 190 has not yet taken place by the Netherlands, on 4 June 2024, the government of the Netherlands explicitly expressed its (re)commitment to ratifying ILO Convention 190 in the short term. Furthermore, the issue of ratification has been put firmly on the agenda of relevant Dutch politicians and government officials. Also, space has been created for global actors to exchange experiences and lessons learned in the fight for ratification. In January 2024, the Netherlands sent in a submission to a call about prostitution and violence against women by the Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls. The submission by the Netherlands highlights that sex work is understood as work and that while violence and exploitation in the sex industry must be addressed - as in any other labour sector - sex work in itself is not considered inherently violent by Dutch law. Although it has not resulted in a positive policy change, possibly also because this parliamentarian left the parliament and the NSC party just months after making this commitment, Dutch parliamentarian Femke Zeedijk did commit to fighting against budget cuts on women's rights in Dutch foreign policy. Being part of a coalition party, thus part of a political party that forms the government in the Netherlands, this commitment had extra weight.

The reporting indicator is unique, considering it takes a long time to influence laws, policies and strategies used at the national level. This will be a 5-year target. The achievement of laws and policies will be counted only once

Formal side event with Dutch MOFA, New Zealand and NSWP on sex work, with sex worker activists from various regions in the panel. Virtual. 1st introductory workshop on sex work (rights & realities) for WO=MEN membership. Participation in and contribution to an informal international advocacy collective aimed at protecting WHRDs in and from Afghanistan and participation of women and girls in peace processes.Knowledge sharing session on extractives, presentation of the toolkit, and exploration of other partners' resources, knowledge, and strategies. Participants: WO=MEN members and relevant actors in and outside of the Netherlands. Lobbied for the Netherlands to ratify ILO C190. Once they have done this, they can promote this convention in international spaces, which they cannot yet do. There has been verbal commitment from the government that they will sign, but we hoped it would still be done before elections in March 2021. We included our CSW recommendations and asked the Minister about them in a public briefing. A follow-up is the CSW66 session with CNV International and labour unions on sex work, which also brought up ILO C190. We ensured ratification by the Netherlands of ILO Convention 190 (C190) on eliminating violence and harassment in the world of work stayed on the agenda of the Dutch government through our inventions at the CSW. We also incorporated sex work into the labour rights perspective. We ensured this by including it in the key recommendations from civil society to the Dutch delegation, in feedback on the draft agreed conclusions and by integrating it into the Formal Side Event at the CSW (online due to the COVID situation) jointly with ILO and CNV International (Duth labour union) and labour unions in Senegal and South Africa and sex workers rights activists. This collaboration with sex workers and labour unions was partly new & partly strengthened thanks to this session. For the first time, ILO and several labour union representatives joined in a CSW Formal Side Event jointly with sex worker rights activists to talk about addressing violence against sex workers, including through ratification of ILO C190 and decriminalisation of sex work.1 UN agency and 3 labour unions (Netherlands, Senegal and South Africa) called for support for labour rights, ending violence against sex workers and the ratification of ILO C190. Key recommendations related to increasing and improving the resourcing of women's and feminist movements were included in civil society recommendations to the Dutch CSW delegation and in various CMI inputs to the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, including the input on the new foreign trade and development cooperation policy and the feminist foreign policy consultations. Several activities including: *liaising with Sint Maarten gov. on sex workers' rights and policy (follow-up from CSW66); interview with Sisonke colleague Kholi about sex workers rights in South Africa; article about sex workers' rights in Kenya in the Feminist Foreign Policy Vice Versa special magazine; WO=MEN signed Manifesto for inclusive EU GBV Policies (by PICUM, ESWA, Amnesty and others) which explicitly mentions and includes sex workers and trans and non-binary people, launched on 8 March; WO=MEN actively sought support from other orgs in our network to support the manifesto as well; WO=MEN gave a presentation on the why feminists need sex workers panel at the ESWA regional conference in October in Brussels; WO=MEN joined the discussion at the European Parliament during the launch of the European Coalition on Sex Workers' Rights and Participation. Several organisations from WO=MEN's network signed on to the Manifesto for inclusive EU GBV policies (by PICUM and others), which explicitly mentions and includes sex workers, trans and gender non-binary people, which have rarely or never before showed public support to sex workers' rights. New allies from the women's and SRHR movement publicly support sex workers and trans rights. WO=MEN also organised an event on the growing anti-gender movement, which included a virtual conversation with Serra Sippel of Fos Feminista about the pushback in the USA. WO=MEN participated in an interview about the Wade vs Roe situation in the USA and about the growing anti-gender movement internationally for Vrij Nederland (summer edition), WO-MEN published a blogpost about it and several WO=MEN colleagues joined the abortion rights march. WO=MEN also signed a statement protecting abortion access in Europe initiated by the Center for Reproductive Rights (July 2023). WO=MEN had a research (masters thesis) done on key organisaitons in the opposition movement in parts of Europe to build knowledge, the researcher - Stephanie - also presented her key findings. WO=MEN had numerous conversations with staff at MoFA and OCW (the ministry responsible for Dutch and European gender equality policy) on the pushback and anti-gender movements, including as part of the CSW66 process and consultation rounds for MoFA and OCW policies. Much work was done re. The influencing of the Funding Framework of the Dutch MFA and Dutch FFP, but these processes are still ongoing. The fact that the Dutch cabinet fell mid-2023 and elections took place in November 2023 with still only a caretaker government in place as coalition negotiations are ongoing has also impacted the opportunities to influence actual laws, policies and strategies as there were few opportunities for such decisions, to happen. .

3 spaces where created at the WTO, CSW and UNFCCC COP: "A new space for women's rights organisations was created following WO=MEN's engagements with the WTO Gender Unit. Concretely, a commitment was made, in the form of a written statement, from WTO working group on Trade & Gender to enable engagement with, among others, women's rights organisations. On 13 February 2024, the co-chairs of the informal working group of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) for Trade & Gender, of which the Netherlands is also a member, mentioned engagement with women's rights organisations in their joint statement as one of the areas of work in which they want to intensify their efforts. The exact words: 'Provide opportunities to engage and consult with external stakeholders such as womenled/owned businesses and entrepreneurs, business networks, civil society and women’s rights organisations on issues pertaining to trade and gender equality'. (the statement can be found here: https://www.tralac.org/documents/resources/external-relations/wto/mc13/5233-joint-statement-on-promoting-inclusive-sustainable-trade-through-gender-equality-13-february-2024/file.html)"A new space was opened for WHRDs, sex worker rights activists specifically, to advise on sex work policy. One of the countries that is part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Sint Maarten, asked WO=MEN to organise a meeting with sex worker leaders who could advise them on sex work policy for their country. This is a result of the years of sex work policy related sessions that CMI has organised, with WO=MEN, together with the Dutch MoFA during the CSW in New York or online. At the UNFCCC COP, feminist climate activists were more able to create and defend spaces for feminist messages, following engagements with experienced CSW activists around strategically organising the ngo-representation, regular strategy meetings, and effectively being able to develop quality mark-ups that are aligned with feminist knowledge of UN language and developments.

The reporting measure of this indicator is unique. If space created or defended has the same agenda/issue and targets the same policy/decision makers, then it will be counted once. At the same time, the space created with a different policy and decision makers will be counted as a different space.
